title: One Axon, Many Dendrites: Neuronal Polarity

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A cell's division into domains that differ in structure and molecules is called {{c1::polarity}}.
cards.quote: Polarity is the word for a cell having two distinct ends or domains that differ in structure and molecules.
cards.section: One cell, two kinds of process

cards.front: Why must a typical vertebrate neuron's dendrites and axon maintain different molecular compositions?
cards.back: Dendrites receive input; the axon carries action potentials to other cells. Their different jobs require different receptors, channels and transport machinery.
cards.quote: The axon is usually single, of even width and often very long; it carries the neuron's output, the action potential, to other cells.
cards.section: One cell, two kinds of process

cards.front: Which microtubule-associated proteins distinguish dendrites from axons in the neuronal polarity description?
cards.back: MAP2 in dendrites; tau in axons.
cards.quote: The axon contains other proteins, such as the microtubule-associated protein tau, and its own channels and vesicle machinery.
cards.section: One cell, two kinds of process

cards.front: The motile tip of a growing neurite is the {{c1::growth cone}}.
cards.quote: Each ends in a growth cone, the motile tip of a growing neurite
cards.section: The map

cards.front: In what order do the five polarization stages occur in dissociated embryonic rat hippocampal neurons?
cards.back: Lamellipodia → similar minor neurites → one rapidly growing axon → dendritic growth and branching → maturation of spines and synapses.
cards.quote: Minor neurites. The veils condense into several short neurites, all alike.
cards.section: Five stages and a race

cards.front: A cultured embryonic rat hippocampal neuron enters {{c1::stage 3}} when one minor neurite begins growing much faster and becomes the axon.
cards.back: This follows the stage of similar minor neurites.
cards.quote: The axon. After a day or two, one neurite starts to grow much faster than the rest. It becomes the axon.
cards.section: Five stages and a race

cards.front: In a young cultured hippocampal neuron, cutting the emerging axon back to its siblings' length sometimes lets another neurite become the axon. What does this rule out?
cards.back: An irrevocably assigned axon identity. Erasing the leader's advantage can let another neurite win, so the early choice remains reversible.
cards.quote: a different neurite, one that would otherwise have become a dendrite, could grow out as the axon.
cards.section: Is it a race? Cut the leader

cards.front: After the emerging axon of a young cultured hippocampal neuron is cut, an uncut sibling is more than about 10 micrometres longer than every other process. Which process should become the axon, and why?
cards.back: The uncut sibling should become the axon. In these young cultured neurons, a sufficient relative length advantage can outweigh a process's previous identity.
cards.quote: When one remaining process, the stump or a sibling, was more than about 10 micrometres longer than all the others, it became the axon.
cards.section: Is it a race? Cut the leader

cards.front: Why does a model that selects one axon need both local positive feedback and competition among neurites?
cards.back: Feedback strengthens a neurite's growth; competition makes that gain limit its rivals. Feedback must also amplify relative advantage beyond simple proportional growth.
cards.quote: Either way, one neurite's gain is the others' loss.
cards.section: What a race with one winner needs

cards.front: In the illustrative neurite model, one process starts at 20 micrometres and four at 15 micrometres. All grow with the same constant fractional rate for 48 hours. What is the final leader-to-sibling length ratio?
cards.back: Let the common growth multiplier be g. The ratio is (20g)/(15g) = 4/3 ≈ 1.33. The leader stays about 33.3% longer; proportional growth alone selects no winner.
cards.quote: All five grow, and the leader stays exactly the same fraction ahead, a third longer than each sibling, for as long as you run the rule.
cards.section: What a race with one winner needs

cards.front: How can a fixed retraction cost help amplify a length advantage in a model where neurites share a limited supply?
cards.back: The same absolute cost consumes a larger fraction of a short neurite's growth. Longer neurites therefore gain a relative advantage beyond proportional allocation alone.
cards.quote: a fixed running cost that every neurite pays, such as retraction, which takes a bigger bite out of a short neurite's growth.
cards.section: What a race with one winner needs

cards.front: Two simulations give five unequal neurites a limited shared supply. One allocates it in proportion to length; the other uses length squared and a fixed retraction cost. Which should sharpen the lead, and what does the comparison test?
cards.back: The second should sharpen the lead and can drive rivals to stubs. The stated rules are competition for supply plus feedback that increases growth relative to length; proportional sharing alone preserves length ratios.
cards.quote: Something must make a long neurite's growth, relative to its own length, larger than a short neurite's.
cards.section: What a race with one winner needs

cards.front: At the future axon's tip, PI3-kinase produces the membrane lipid {{c1::PIP3}}, which recruits proteins with PH domains.
cards.quote: PI3-kinase makes the lipid PIP3, a mark at one spot on the membrane that draws proteins with PH domains to that spot
cards.section: The players, sorted by job

cards.front: In the proposed axon-tip feedback loop, why do actin loosening and microtubule stabilization have complementary effects?
cards.back: Loosened actin is proposed to let microtubules advance into the growth cone, while more stable microtubules support the future axon's extension.
cards.quote: two polymers with opposite jobs at the tip, one giving way, the other advancing.
cards.section: The players, sorted by job

cards.front: Which polarity complex gathers at the tip of the future axon in cultured neurons?
cards.back: The Par3/Par6/aPKC complex.
cards.quote: The Par3/Par6/aPKC complex, the same polarity complex that marks the top of an epithelial cell, gathers there.
cards.section: The players, sorted by job

cards.front: How do Cdc42 and Rac contrast with RhoA in the proposed neurite-growth machinery?
cards.back: GTP-bound Cdc42 and Rac reorganize actin at the tip; RhoA tends to oppose neurite growth.
cards.quote: the Rho-family GTPases Cdc42 and Rac, molecular switches that are on when bound to GTP
cards.section: The players, sorted by job

cards.front: All minor neurites of a stage 2 cultured hippocampal neuron receive a PI3-kinase inhibitor. What should happen to axon formation, and why?
cards.back: No neurite is expected to become an axon, as reported for this treatment. Blocking PIP3 production prevents the proposed positive loop from giving a neurite its winning boost.
cards.quote: Blocking PI3-kinase throughout is reported to do the opposite: no neurite becomes an axon.
cards.section: Rig the race

cards.front: Before axon choice in cultured hippocampal neurons, locally interfering with actin assembly at one growth cone makes that neurite more likely to become the axon. Why is this stronger evidence than simply observing loose actin in the future axon?
cards.back: The intervention precedes and biases the choice, supporting a causal contribution of local actin loosening. Observation alone cannot distinguish a cause of axon choice from its consequence.
cards.quote: The treated neurite was likely to become the axon.
cards.section: Rig the race

cards.front: A light-activated taxol analogue is released in one neurite of a stage 2 cultured hippocampal neuron. What happens to its chance of becoming the axon, and why?
cards.back: Its chance increases. Local microtubule stabilization can bias the competition toward that neurite, consistent with the future axon's more stable microtubules.
cards.quote: Releasing a light-activated taxol analogue in one neurite made that neurite more likely to become the axon
cards.section: Rig the race

cards.front: Whole-cell actin disruption or low-dose taxol can produce several axons in cultured neurons. Why does this challenge an explanation based only on accelerating the competitive race model?
cards.back: The stated full model still selects one winner when supply increases or all rates scale together. A possible extension is that global cytoskeletal changes let several neurites acquire axonal features without winning; that interpretation remains untested by the model.
cards.quote: The whole-cell drug results are therefore not what a simple across-the-board speed-up of this model predicts.
cards.section: Rig the race

cards.front: On microtubules, most kinesins move toward plus ends, whereas {{c1::dynein}} moves toward minus ends.
cards.quote: Most kinesins walk toward plus ends; dynein walks toward minus ends.
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: How does microtubule orientation differ between axons and dendrites in cultured rat hippocampal neurons?
cards.back: Axons have nearly all plus-end-out microtubules; dendrites have mixed orientations, with substantial fractions pointing each way.
cards.quote: In the axon, nearly all microtubules point their plus ends away from the cell body. In dendrites the orientation is mixed
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: Why can a minus-end-directed motor carry cargo away from the cell body on some dendritic microtubules?
cards.back: On minus-end-out tracks, the minus end lies away from the cell body. Moving toward that end therefore carries cargo outward.
cards.quote: Cargo carried by dynein can travel outward only on minus-end-out tracks
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: A cargo switches from a plus-end-directed kinesin to dynein while staying on the same plus-end-out axonal microtubule. What happens to its direction, and why?
cards.back: It reverses from outward travel to movement toward the cell body. The track's plus end is outward, and dynein moves toward its inward-facing minus end.
cards.quote: Most kinesins walk toward plus ends; dynein walks toward minus ends.
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: An idealized track count finds 196 of 200 axonal and 66 of 120 dendritic microtubules plus-end-out. How many times larger is the fraction permitting outward dynein motion in the dendrite? Assume track orientation alone determines eligibility.
cards.back: Outward dynein needs minus-end-out tracks: axon (200−196)/200 = 2%; dendrite (120−66)/120 = 45%. The fraction ratio is 45/2 = 22.5. This compares eligible tracks, not measured cargo flux.
cards.quote: Cargo carried by dynein can travel outward only on minus-end-out tracks, which vertebrate dendrites have in large numbers and the axon almost lacks.
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: A rapidly extending neurite develops stable, plus-end-out microtubules. How could transport reinforce both its growth lead and its later molecular identity in the proposed polarity model?
cards.back: The growth-feedback rule says faster growth draws more building material and transport. The sorting rule says a kinesin preferring stable plus-end-out tracks can favor the axon. Together, these could reinforce extension and selective cargo delivery.
cards.quote: a kinesin that prefers stable plus-end-out microtubules can be steered into the axon.
cards.section: Tracks that point two ways

cards.front: What is the main scaffold of the axon initial segment (AIS)?
cards.back: Ankyrin G.
cards.why: It binds beta-IV spectrin and, through ANK repeats, sodium channels, KCNQ2/3 channels and neurofascin-186. Spectrin links the scaffold to actin rings.
cards.quote: Under its membrane sits a dense coat built on the scaffold ankyrin G.
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: Why does the axon initial segment often initiate action potentials after inputs reach the dendrites and cell body?
cards.back: Its high sodium-channel density, among other features, gives it a low threshold for initiating an action potential in many neurons.
cards.quote: A high density of sodium channels, among other features, gives it a low threshold
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: Laser-trap experiments found membrane proteins mobile on the soma and dendrites but restrained at the initial segment, with restraint depending on actin. What polarity mechanism does this support?
cards.back: An actin-dependent barrier to membrane-protein movement at the initial segment. This supports restricted mixing between membrane domains without establishing the barrier's precise mechanism.
cards.quote: they moved freely in the cell body and dendrites but were held back at the initial segment, and that the hold depended on actin.
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: A neuronal scaffold is removed only after an axon and initial segment have formed. The proximal axon then gains dendritic features. Does the timing test establishment or maintenance of polarity, and why?
cards.back: Maintenance: polarity was already established before removal. The result shows that preserving axonal identity requires an ongoing scaffold function; it does not test the initial choice.
cards.quote: Because the axon was already chosen, the experiment tests maintenance, not choice: identity has to be actively held.
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: Ankyrin G is lowered after the initial segment forms in cultured hippocampal neurons. What should happen to MAP2 exclusion and the proximal axon's appearance, and why?
cards.back: MAP2 can enter the axon, and the proximal axon can develop dendritic spines as the AIS disassembles. Ankyrin G is needed to maintain this local axonal domain.
cards.quote: The AIS fell apart, and MAP2 spread into the axon. Near the cell body the axon began to look like a dendrite
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: After ankyrin G knockdown dismantles the initial segment in cultured hippocampal neurons, should loss of axonal features necessarily extend uniformly to the distal axon? Explain.
cards.back: No. The distal axon can retain axonal proteins despite proximal changes. The reported regional difference implies additional maintenance mechanisms, which these experiments do not identify.
cards.quote: The AIS holds the proximal axon; the distal axon keeps its features without it
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: An actin-dependent barrier restrains membrane proteins at an axon's start. Does that alone explain exclusion of a microtubule-bound cytoplasmic marker? What comparison would test whether both depend on the same actin requirement?
cards.back: No: membrane diffusion and intracellular cargo localization are distinct. Compare membrane mobility and cytoplasmic-marker exclusion with and without actin disruption. The stated barrier evidence directly tests only membrane movement; shared sensitivity would support, but not prove, a common mechanism.
cards.quote: the hold reaches beyond the membrane that the laser trap tested; how the segment keeps MAP2 out is not settled.
cards.section: The initial segment: a gate that holds the win

cards.front: In fully polarized mouse hippocampal cultures, compare cutting an axon to a stump shorter than about 35 micrometres with leaving a long stump. What usually grows as the axon, and why?
cards.back: A close cut can let a dendrite become the axon; a distant cut usually lets the original stump regrow. A long stump retains an axonal advantage, linked by the authors to stable microtubules.
cards.quote: remove nearly all of the axon and the label can be reassigned; leave enough of it and the axon simply repairs itself.
cards.section: Design problem: the mature neuron's cut

cards.front: Why is competition after a close axon cut in a mature cultured neuron only analogous to stage 2, rather than a return to the same developmental starting point?
cards.back: The remaining processes are already mature dendrites. Extensive axon removal can reopen competition, but the neuron has already built structures that help maintain axonal identity.
cards.quote: Now no process has a clear axonal advantage, which is a little like stage 2, though the dendrites are mature.
cards.section: Design problem: the mature neuron's cut

cards.front: How could you test whether an intact initial segment contributes to the old axon's advantage after a distant cut in mature hippocampal cultures, given that distal microtubules may also preserve identity?
cards.back: Compare matched long-stump cuts with and without prior ankyrin G reduction, scoring stump regrowth versus dendritic takeover. The stated rules assign proximal maintenance to the AIS and possible distal memory to stable microtubules. Extra takeover would support an AIS contribution, not establish exclusivity.
cards.quote: lower ankyrin G first, then make the distant cut, and ask whether a dendrite now competes with the regrowing stump.
cards.section: Design problem: the mature neuron's cut

cards.front: Why should equal starting neurites in dissociated cultures not be assumed to describe the starting conditions of neurons developing in tissue?
cards.back: Dissociation removes neighbours and developmental history. In tissue, migration can already set polarity, and environmental cues orient the machinery, tilting or bypassing the competition.
cards.quote: In the brain many neurons arrive with polarity already set by their migration, so the race may be tilted or skipped.
cards.section: Does the brain run the same race?

cards.front: Developing mouse cortical neurons lack LKB1 or both SAD-A and SAD-B. Should tissue cues alone be expected to rescue axon formation, and why?
cards.back: No: most of these neurons fail to form axons despite developing in tissue. The LKB1–SAD pathway is required in developing mouse cortex, even though tissue changes the starting conditions for polarization.
cards.quote: Cortical neurons lacking LKB1, or both SAD kinases, fail to form axons.
cards.section: Does the brain run the same race?

cards.front: Why should the young-neuron length lead and mature-neuron stump threshold from hippocampal cultures not be treated as universal neuronal constants?
cards.back: They are thresholds from specific cultures. The model's apparent threshold depends on growth noise, feedback strength and how winning is defined, so its position can change.
cards.quote: where it sits depends on how noisy growth is, how steep the feedback is and how a winner is defined.
cards.section: Length thresholds in the cut-axon experiments

cards.front: How would repeated live imaging distinguish whether uniform axonal microtubule orientation develops during axon choice or only after it? Would observing early uniformity prove it causes axon choice?
cards.back: Track orientation and neurite growth in the same cell before, during and after one process pulls ahead. The stated rules link tracks to cargo sorting and growth competition. Early uniformity supports involvement during choice, but temporal association alone cannot establish causation.
cards.quote: the uniform plus-end-out array forming as the axon forms.
cards.section: When do the tracks sort?
